name: Rating-photo standards

card.summary: Community conventions for taking neutral front and side photos so that face and body ratings are comparable, giving users feedback based on how they actually look rather than on a flattering angle.
card.note: Wide-angle close-ups and lighting change how a face appears, which is the reason forums publish photo rules.

quick.overview:
Rating-photo standards are the informal rules that looksmaxxing forums publish for the pictures users post when asking for a rating or critique. They usually ask for a neutral expression, a straight-on front view and a true side profile, even lighting and a camera held at eye level at some distance.

The payoff is feedback that reflects a person's real features. Because a close-up from below, a tilted head or heavy filter changes how the nose, jaw and eyes look, standardised photos let raters and the poster compare like with like, and let a user track changes in their face over time.
quick.how: Forum guides typically describe taking the front and side photos against a plain background, with the face relaxed, hair back, and no filters or heavy editing. Many ask for the camera to be at eye height and a few steps away, sometimes zoomed in, rather than a close selfie. Users often repeat the same setup later to produce before and after comparisons.
quick.risks: The main practical risk is privacy: photos posted on public forums can be saved or shared, and raters' opinions are subjective. Researchers on facial perception also report that camera distance, angle and lighting alter perceived features, which is why unstandardised photos can give misleading feedback.

lead: Rating-photo standards are the posting conventions that looksmaxxing communities use for pictures submitted to face-rating or critique sections. They specify how a front view and a side profile should be taken so that raters see comparable images. The aim is feedback that reflects a person's real features and a repeatable template for tracking changes in grooming, skin, hair, weight or procedures.[1]

Forum rating culture grew from the early PSL forums, which used numeric scales and shared jargon for judging faces.[1] Camera geometry is the technical reason behind the rules: a 2018 modelling study found that at about 12 inches a nose can appear roughly 30 percent larger relative to the face than in a distant image, with the difference negligible at 5 feet.[2]

chain: Take neutral, consistently framed front and side photos
Raters see features without angle or lens distortion
More comparable feedback and trackable before-and-after changes
angle.text: Standardised photos give a user a consistent record of their face. Feedback can then focus on grooming, skin, hair, facial hair and other changeable features, and progress can be compared between photos taken under the same conditions.

infobox: Neutral expression, even light, eye-level camera, no filters

paras: Forum rating sections typically ask for at least two images: a straight-on front view and a side profile, often with a smiling photo as an optional third. Guides describe a relaxed neutral face, hair pulled away from the forehead and ears, no sunglasses or hats, and plain lighting from the front or a window rather than from above or below.

A recurring element is camera placement. Guides advise eye-level height and a moderate distance, because a phone held close and below the face enlarges the nose and chin relative to the rest of the face and can change how the jaw and midface read.

The photo-distance concern is documented in plastic surgery research. Rutgers and Stanford authors modelled average male and female faces and found that wide-angle close-ups enlarge the nose and central features, a pattern they said does not represent the true three-dimensional shape.[2]

The standards serve two functions: they let strangers rate or critique a face on equal terms, and they give users a repeatable template for tracking changes from skincare, haircuts, weight change, grooming or procedures. Moderators in rating sections commonly remove or ask for a retake of photos that are heavily filtered or angled.

Rating sections sit within the wider culture of scales such as PSL, in which raters assess features like jawline and canthal tilt; Wikipedia notes that commentators describe such scales as pseudoscientific.[1]

No studies found. Related work is limited to a modelling study of how camera distance alters the apparent proportions of the nose, which did not analyse photographs of real people or forum ratings.[2]
